text.p: The Democratic Party has returned a $325,000 donation from a man who said he was a distant relative of India's late leader Mahatma Gandhi because the source of the money could not be verified, a party official said on Thursday.

Party spokeswoman Amy Weiss Tobe said it sent a check on Wednesday by overnight express delivery to the donor, Yogesh Gandhi of Orinda, California. It was one of the largest and most controversial donations the party had received.
Campaign contributions by foreigners became an issue in the presidential campaign after donations from some people with ties to foreign business interests in Indonesia, Taiwan and South Korea.

After questions were raised about the Gandhi donation, Tobe said, a party official on Monday contacted Gandhi, who heads the Gandhi Memorial International Foundation in Orinda, to determine the source of the money.

The money was given at a May fundraiser in Washington attended by President Bill Clinton. It is illegal for foreign companies or nationals to give campaign donations but legal residents, such as Gandhi, are not included in the ban.

"We contacted him and asked specifically whether the funds were his and questioned him about a court transcript where he said he had no assets, and he said that he could prove to us in fact that he did have money, but he never got back to us," Tobe said.
She referred to a court case in August by a former employee of Gandhi's foundation who sought $3,046 in back pay. During the proceeding, Gandhi said he had no money.
After Gandhi did not return the telephone call, Tobe said, the party decided to send back the money "when there were so many unanswered questions."

At the May fundraiser where Gandhi gave the money, he brought along a "life-sized bust" of Mahatma Gandhi and asked that he be allowed to present it -- the "Gandhi peace prize" to Clinton. She said the bust was given to Clinton, adding that Gandhi had given similar awards to others including former President Ronald Reagan and missionary Mother Teresa.

This was not the first donation the Democrats have returned but it could be the largest. The party returned $250,000 after it was found that the money came from a South Korean firm in violation of a law against foreign contributions, another $10,000 given by a South Korean national and $20,000 -- donated to the Treasury -- that had been given to the Democrats by a convicted drug smuggler.

Unsuccessful Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole has accused Clinton's party of selling access to Clinton and the White House through foreign-linked donations generated in part by a Democratic Party fundraiser, John Huang.

Republicans in Congress have said they will investigate the donations and activities of Huang, a former official of the giant Indonesian bank combine, Lippo Group, who became a Commerce Department official before moving to the Democratic National Committee to raise money from Asian American groups.
Democrats reject charges the party has accepted illegal donations and say the Republicans accepted similar donations.
